Personal hobbies

Building something useful, close to home.

Electronics has been a personal interest since childhood. One of my most meaningful projects began with a familiar problem in the farming community where I grew up.

Independent project · Started in 2020

A GSM controller for irrigation pumps in the Krishna River basin

Remote operation and status updates from an ordinary mobile phone, using SMS without an internet connection.

3–4prototype installations evaluated over months
SMScommands and operating-status updates
Custom PCBdeveloped after the modular field prototypes

A phone message instead of another trip

During the COVID-19 period in 2020, I saw farmers making repeated trips to remote pump installations to check the electricity supply, start irrigation, or investigate a stopped motor. Some pumps carried water several kilometres from the river, and an unreliable power schedule could mean another journey at night or in heavy rain.

I wanted to make that routine easier using equipment farmers already owned. I studied the existing starter panels, then built a controller around an Arduino, a SIM800L cellular module, relay interfaces, and current and supply-state sensors. I wrote the embedded C/C++ firmware to receive SMS commands and report the pump’s operating condition.

The controller interfaced with the starter’s low-power control circuit while retaining its contactors and existing protections. This made it possible to retrofit the system to the installations I was testing.

More than a remote switch

A command to start a motor is only useful if the farmer can tell what happened next. I added current monitoring, timed operation, automatic and manual modes, and messages about power restoration and motor status. Settings were retained in EEPROM so a power interruption did not erase the selected mode.

The firmware checked supply readiness and coordinated its timing with the existing starter. Current measurements helped flag possible low-load, dry-running, or overload conditions. Repeated abnormal readings could trigger a stop command and an SMS alert, giving more information than relay state alone.

I assembled and evaluated approximately three to four prototypes over months of field operation, including installations with roughly 10 HP centrifugal pumps. These trials demonstrated practical remote operation and revealed the electrical disturbances the design needed to tolerate.

The field became the test bench

The first difficult problem appeared during motor-starter switching: electronics that worked on the bench could reset near the contactors. Cellular transmission added short bursts of current demand, making the power supply another part of the debugging process.

I investigated switching disturbances and voltage drops, then worked through regulation, filtering, local energy storage, decoupling, and suppression of inductive transients. These changes substantially improved prototype stability. I also refined the sensing and timing logic to work with the start-ready signals of the particular starter configurations in the field.

The lesson was practical: communication, sensing, firmware, and power integrity had to work together under the conditions at the pump, not just under a stable laboratory supply.

From separate modules to a purpose-built board

Once the modular prototypes had demonstrated the concept, I designed a custom PCB to reduce wiring, assembly complexity, and dependence on separate breakout boards. It brought together an ATmega328P microcontroller, a replaceable GSM-module interface, four relay channels, power conversion, sensing connections, and external terminals.

I prepared the schematic and layout, ordered the boards, assembled the components, and tested programming, communication, and relay operation. Board bring-up exposed another useful problem: relays worked with an external regulated supply but flickered with the initial onboard supply configuration. I traced voltage levels and investigated power distribution, return paths, and transient loading.

The field-tested modular system established the feasibility of the approach. The integrated PCB demonstrated the core architecture and identified the power-system revisions needed for a more reliable next version. Taking the project through electronics, firmware, field integration, and board testing remains an important part of how I learned to engineer complete systems.

Away from the workbench
